name: Crom Dubh

attributes.attribute: an Irish god or hero who appears as a pagan king in the legends of St. Patrick
converted after Patrick’s written thanks weighed the same as the three bulls
his name titles the annual celebration at Croagh Patrick
site of the annual celebration named Crom Dubh, in Co. Mayo
sometimes the name of Patrick’s kingly adversary, possibly a humanized god

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Crom Dubh turns up in the tales of St. Patrick as a god or hero of Ireland. There he wears the face of a pagan king. Patrick once received a present of three bulls, yet failed, in Crom Dubh's view, to thank him well enough. At the arrival of each beast the saint merely said thanks to god. Patrick then jotted his words onto separate slips of paper, three in all, and weighed them against the bulls. The two measures came out equal, and Crom Dubh converted on the spot. Crom Dubh's name lives on in the yearly festival held at Croagh Patrick in Co. Mayo. People at times call Patrick's royal foe Crom Cruach, a sign that this king was an old god dressed in human form.

okr.objective: Crom Dubh is a pagan king in St. Patrick’s legends who converts after a test with three bulls.
key_results: He appears as a pagan king who grew angry that Patrick gave only “thanks to god” for three bulls.
Patrick’s written thanks weighed the same as the bulls, and Crom Dubh converted.
His name titles the annual celebration at Croagh Patrick in Co. Mayo; the adversary is sometimes called Crom Cruach.
